conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this. I’m Dr. Martin, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into new motherhood.

Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It can flag anything from the normal “baby blues” to something that might need extra care, including anxiety or thoughts of self-harm. Your answers stay between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about safety; then we work together on next steps.

There are no right or wrong answers, and this isn’t a test of your parenting—just a snapshot of your emotional well-being so we know how best to support you. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions one by one. I’ll ask them conversationally; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace.

Shall we begin?

In the past seven days, how often have you felt cheerful or able to enjoy things—would you say all of the time, some of the time, occasionally, or never?
I’d say…some of the time. When the baby smiles or when I get a quiet minute to myself I can still feel that spark, but it’s definitely not every moment.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not as easily as before, but if my partner or my sister cracks a joke I catch myself giggling. It’s just that sometimes the laugh feels a little quick to fade, like the tiredness creeps right back in.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to stuff—like taking the baby for walks or having coffee with a friend—but the excitement is kind of muted. I still mark things on the calendar, it just feels more “nice” than “can’t-wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really, no. If the baby’s fussy or I’m running late, I figure it’s just part of the chaos right now. I might think, “I should’ve started sooner,” but I don’t stay stuck on it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah. Most nights I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing okay or if that tiny cough meant something serious, even though everything looked fine at the last check-up. It’s not constant, just these quick waves of worry that pop up out of nowhere and then settle.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not panicky, no. There’s the odd moment when I hear a siren or the baby gives a sudden cry and my heart jumps, but it passes in seconds. I haven’t had that overwhelming scared feeling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like when laundry’s piled up and the baby needs feeding and the dog’s barking all at once. I feel a bit swamped for a minute, but I take a breath, make a list, and chip away at it. It doesn’t stay heavy for long.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I wouldn’t say that. My mood’s pretty steady, and once the baby settles for the night I can usually fall asleep without trouble.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t really felt sad or miserable overall. I get tired and a bit overwhelmed sometimes, but that heavy, down-in-the-dumps feeling hasn’t shown up.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried like that. I might get a little teary when I’m super tired, but it’s rare and passes quickly.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 8: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed  
- Mild anhedonia: laughter and anticipatory enjoyment present but muted  
- Transient, situational anxiety (nocturnal worries about infant health, startle response to sudden noises)  
- Occasional feeling of being “swamped” by concurrent demands; resolves with planning  

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, sleep-onset problems linked to mood, guilt/worthlessness, panic spells, self-harm ideation  

Pattern  
Overall mood remains stable; affect brightens with social contact. No neuro-vegetative signs of depression; anxiety is episodic and contextual, not pervasive.

Screening significance  
Findings fall below threshold for probable major postpartum depression; mild anxiety symptoms noted. No current safety concerns.

Recommendation  
Continue routine postpartum monitoring; educate on red-flag mood/anxiety changes; return for re-screen if symptoms intensify or persist ≥2 weeks.
